name: Ahimelech
title: High Priest of Nob
summary: Achimelech, son of Ahitub, was the high priest in the priestly town of Nob and belonged to Eli's priestly line through the Ithamar branch. His fate is inseparably linked to the conflict between Saul and David. When David arrived at Nob as a fugitive, Achimelech gave him, in good faith, the bread of the Presence from the sanctuary and Goliath's sword. The Edomite Doeg, who witnessed the event, accused Achimelech before Saul. Despite Achimelech defending his innocence by pointing to David's loyalty and position as the king's son-in-law, Saul sentenced him and all the priests of Nob to death. When the king's own soldiers refused to raise their hands against the Lord's anointed priests, Doeg himself carried out the dreadful massacre and killed 85 priests. This event marks a turning point in Saul's moral decline and can be understood as a partial fulfillment of the prophecy concerning judgment on Eli's house. Achimelech's son Abiathar survived as the only priest and joined David. The account of the bread of the Presence was later used by Jesus to illustrate that mercy and human need outweigh ceremonial regulations.
roles: keeper of the tabernacle at Nob

keyEvents.title: Ahimelech Helps David at Nob
keyEvents.description: When David fled from Saul, he came to the priestly city of Nob where the high priest Ahimelech gave him holy bread to eat and the sword of Goliath.

keyEvents.title: Doeg Sees David with Ahimelech
keyEvents.description: The Edomite Doeg, one of Saul's servants, was present at Nob and witnessed Ahimelech helping David.

keyEvents.title: Doeg Accuses Ahimelech before Saul
keyEvents.description: Doeg reported to King Saul that Ahimelech had helped David with food and weapons, which aroused the king's fury.

keyEvents.title: Ahimelech Defends Himself Before Saul
keyEvents.description: When Saul summoned Ahimelech and the priests from Nob, Ahimelech defended himself by pointing out that David was the king's faithful servant and son-in-law, and that he knew of no conflict between David and the king.

keyEvents.title: The Massacre of the Priests at Nob
keyEvents.description: Saul ordered the execution of Ahimelech and all the priests in Nob. When the king's own men refused to lay hands on the Lord's priests, the Edomite Doeg carried out the massacre, killing 85 priests who wore linen ephods.

keyEvents.title: Jesus Refers to the Event with the Showbread
keyEvents.description: Jesus referred to how David received the showbread from the priest at Nob as an example that human needs can take precedence over ceremonial regulations. The event is recorded in all three Synoptic Gospels.

versions.summary: Ahimelech was a priest in the city of Nob who helped David when he fled from King Saul. He gave David holy bread and the sword of Goliath, unaware that David was on the run. As a result, he and 85 other priests were killed on Saul's orders by the Edomite Doeg.
versions.title: The Priest at Nob
versions.reason: [minor] In Mark 2:26, Jesus mentions the priest as 'Abjatar' (Ebjatar), not Ahimelech. This is a well-known textual critical issue. The description should reflect this nuance to be precise.; [major] The profile lacks footnotes. There are several interesting historical, linguistic, and theological aspects regarding Ahimelech that deserve elaboration: the meaning of his name, the textual critical issue in Mark 2:26, Nob as a priestly city, and the massacre in light of Saul's mental decline.; [minor] Ahimelech was not only a priest but served as high priest in Nob. He had responsibility for the showbread and the sanctuary, indicating a leadership position among the priests.; [minor] The summary is good, but could be strengthened by noting that Ahimelech belonged to the line of Eli and that the massacre at Nob can be seen as a fulfillment of the prophecy against the house of Eli (1 Sam 2:31-36).

As a result, Ahimelech and 85 other priests were killed at Saul's command, carried out by Doeg. The massacre can be seen as a partial fulfillment of the prophecy against Eli's house. Only Ahimelech's son Abiathar survived and became David's priest. Jesus later referred to the incident with the showbread as an example that human needs can take precedence over ceremonial laws.

versions.reason: [minor] The title 'The Priest at Nob' is accurate but could be more descriptive. Since Ahimelech was the high priest (not just an ordinary priest), the title could reflect this better. Suggests 'The High Priest at Nob'.; [minor] The description of Jesus' reference is good and covers the Markan problem, but it could also include references to Matthew 12:3-4 and Luke 6:3-4 for completeness, since all three Synoptics record this event.

versions.summary: Ahimelech was the high priest in the city of Nob and a descendant of Eli through the line of Ithamar. When David was fleeing from King Saul, he went to Ahimelech at Nob, where the priest innocently gave him the bread of the Presence and the sword of Goliath. Doeg the Edomite, who was present, reported this to Saul. The enraged king summoned Ahimelech and the priests of Nob, and despite Ahimelech's defense, Saul ordered them all executed. When Saul's own men refused to lay hands on the Lord's priests, Doeg carried out the massacre and killed 85 priests. This tragedy can be understood as a partial fulfillment of the judgment against Eli's house. Ahimelech's son Abiathar was the only one who survived and fled to David, where he served as priest. The incident with the bread of the Presence was later used by Jesus as an example that mercy and human need outweigh ceremonial regulations.

footnotes.text: The name Ahimelech (Hebrew: אֲחִימֶלֶךְ, Ahimelekh) means 'my brother is king' or 'brother of the king'. The royal connotation of the name is ironic given that Ahimelech was killed precisely because of a king's suspicion.

In Mark 2:26, Jesus refers to the event with the showbread but mentions the priest as 'Abiathar' (Ebiatar), Ahimelech's son. This has been the subject of much discussion. Some scholars believe it may be a textual variant, while others suggest that the phrase 'in the days of Abiathar the high priest' is a chronological marker rather than an identification of who actually gave the bread.

Nob was a priestly city near Jerusalem, likely on the Mount of Olives or in the area between Anathoth and Jerusalem. After the destruction of Shiloh, the tabernacle and its holy objects were apparently moved there. The city served as a temporary religious center during the transitional period between the time of the judges and the building of the temple.

The massacre at Nob, where 85 priests were killed, can be seen as a partial fulfillment of the prophecy against Eli's house in 1 Samuel 2:31–36. Ahimelech was a descendant of Eli through the line of Ithamar, and this tragedy marks the near-total collapse of that priestly lineage. Only Abiathar survived and continued serving as a priest under David.

Doeg's role as Saul's shepherd and an Edomite who carried out the massacre is remarkable. In rabbinic tradition (Talmud, Sanhedrin 106b), Doeg is portrayed as a learned man who was nonetheless morally corrupt. Psalm 52 is traditionally linked to this event, with its superscription referring to Doeg's betrayal.

The 85 priests who were killed all wore linen ephods. The fact that Saul's own soldiers refused to lay hands on the Lord's priests, while Doeg—an Edomite and thus an outsider—willingly carried out the order, underscores the severity of Saul's sin and his growing isolation from Israel's religious and military leadership.

The showbread (Hebrew: לֶחֶם הַפָּנִים, lechem hapanim, 'bread of the presence') consisted of twelve loaves placed before the Lord in the sanctuary every Sabbath. According to the law, only priests were permitted to eat them (Lev 24:5–9). The fact that Ahimelech gave them to David and his men shows a situation where necessity was regarded as more important than the ritual regulation.

Ahimelech is also mentioned in Psalm 34, whose superscription refers to the event when David pretended to be insane before Abimelech (Achish). The name 'Abimelech' in the psalm's title has led to discussion about the relationship between the names Ahimelech and Abimelech; while linguistically closely related, they refer to different individuals.
